name: Correlation-meter-guided widening: Haas fails mono (comb filter), stereo phaser + M/S side gain, linear vs detuning chorus, and a per-band width map (mono lows, moderate low-mids, widest upper mids, restrained highs)
goal: Widen a mono or narrow synth/pad while staying mono-safe, judging every move on a correlation meter/vectorscope (+1 = mono, 0 = fully independent L/R = widest safe, below 0 = cancels in mono). Reject pure Haas widening because a fixed one-channel delay is a comb filter when summed to mono. Create stereo with a stereo phaser (different delay/filtering per channel) and then scale width with mid/side side-gain. Choose linear (non-detuning) chorus for natural instruments/classic synths and detuning (supersaw-style) chorus to thicken thin digital synths. Finish with a multiband width map: lows (below ~100-300 Hz) mono, low-mids up to ~1.6 kHz slightly narrower, upper mids widest (correlation touching but not crossing 0), highs/transients not too wide. Delta vs the stereo-width cluster: the correlation-meter target per band and the phaser-then-M/S widening path.
prerequisites: A DAW with a correlation meter / vectorscope on the bus or track
A stereo phaser, a chorus (linear) and a detune/unison-style chorus, a mid/side utility, a multiband (3-4 band) stereo width tool

inputs.name: source
inputs.description: Mono or narrow synth/pad/lead to widen

inputs.name: mix_context
inputs.description: Rest of the mix with bass and drums, for the final check

outputs.name: widened_part
outputs.description: Wider part whose correlation stays >= 0 and that holds its tone in mono

outputs.name: width_map
outputs.description: Band split points and width per band used

constraints: Correlation is the measure: never let the bus or the widened part sit below 0 for long; below 0 means the channels cancel when summed to mono.
Pure Haas (fixed delay on one channel) is rejected here: mono-summed it is a comb filter with a fixed notch pattern the ear spots as unnatural.
Chorus modulates delay time, so keep depth subtle on sustained pads so pitch stays steady (Matt dislikes wobbly pitch); prefer the phaser + side-gain route on held chords.
Band split values (~100-300 Hz, ~1.6 kHz) are the presenter's personal starting points, not universal; tune by ear and meter.
Best width comes from wide source material (e.g. real double-takes); these tools only create or rebalance width from a mono/narrow source.
Ableton/MIDI-friendly: device names map to stock Live devices or generic modules; patterns are plain MIDI clips.

Original synthesis/processing recipe; not affiliated with Ableton, Reason, Bitwig, Soundtoys, FabFilter, Eventide or any vendor. Map product devices to generic modules (sampler, noise osc, filter, envelope, LFO, EQ, saturator, compressor, delay, reverb) in any DAW, hardware or Web Audio.
Steady pitch: no random pitch wobble or randomised notes; no rapid clicking textures (Matt's preference).

steps.action: Put a correlation meter / vectorscope on the part. Read it: +1 = identical channels (mono), 0 = fully independent (maximum safe width), negative = opposite polarity that will cancel in mono. Mono-sum a very wide source to hear the change (a negative-correlation choir changed tone audibly; a moderately wide supersaw barely changed).
steps.expect: You can predict mono loss from the meter

steps.action: Test pure Haas: delay one channel by a fixed few ms, then mono-sum. Hear the comb-filter colour (it behaves like a comb-filter device). Do not use this as the widening method.
Create real stereo from mono with a stereo phaser (default settings are a fine start): each channel gets different delay/filtering, so the meter leaves +1 while keeping the phaser character modest.
steps.expect: Correlation drops below +1; part is now stereo

steps.action: Scale the width with mid/side: split into mid (common to L and R) and side (difference), and raise or lower only the side gain. Compare wet/dry: the core tone should stay the same because only existing content is boosted or cut.
steps.expect: Width adjustable without changing the sound's heart

steps.action: Pick the chorus type: a linear (non-detuning) chorus for natural instruments or classic synth leads, which only gets a bit quieter in mono; a detuning/unison-style spread chorus for thin, harsh digital synths that need thickening (it changes a little in mono but does not collapse).
steps.expect: Width + thickness matched to the source type

steps.action: Apply a multiband width map: split at ~100 Hz (try 100-300 Hz) and keep that band mono; low-mids up to ~1.6 kHz a little narrower but still solid; upper mids the widest, pushed until correlation touches 0 but does not cross it; highs (mostly transients) not too wide so they do not vanish in mono.
steps.expect: Part reads wide in a full mix while the meter stays >= 0

steps.action: Check in the full mix with bass and drums and in mono, then trim band widths.

verification: Correlation meter on the processed part stays >= 0 throughout playback.
Band below the low split reads ~+1 (mono).
Mono sum shows no comb-filter notch pattern and level drop of the part is small (about 3 dB or less).
